title: Anisotropic Spectral Error Dressing for Calibrated Ensemble Weather Forecasts

**Purpose:**  
No prior paper explicitly establishes the directional (anisotropic) structure of AI weather forecast errors. While [1] discusses anisotropy in precipitation forecasts, it does not address AI-driven weather forecasts or residual error anisotropy. Similarly, [22] analyzes anisotropy in sea surface height spectra, but this is unrelated to AI forecast errors. None of the other papers report or establish the same empirical relationship.  

**Mechanism:**  
The mechanism involves computing a calibration anisotropy index \( A_{cal} \) from spherical-harmonic coefficients of residuals, partitioning modes into zonal and meridional bins using the normalized order ratio \( \mu = |m|/l \). [23] proposes a test for isotropy on a sphere using spherical harmonic functions, which is substantively equivalent to the spherical harmonic decomposition and anisotropy analysis used here. [13] also employs spherical harmonics for anisotropy analysis, though in a different domain. Both papers cover the mechanism at the primitive level.  

**Evaluation:**  
The evaluation design involves analyzing \( A_{cal} \), power ratios, and synoptic-scale anisotropy using spherical harmonics. [23] uses spherical harmonics to test isotropy on a sphere, which matches the evaluation design at the benchmark family level. [13] similarly evaluates anisotropy using spherical harmonics, covering the design. The specific metrics and thresholds (e.g., \( A_{cal} = -0.276 \)) are new instances but do not constitute a new evaluation design.  

**Domain:**  
The domain is data-driven weather forecasting and forecast error spectral analysis. [6], [7], [9], and [21] all address numerical weather prediction or data-driven forecasting, covering the general application area. While this contribution focuses on error spectral analysis, that is a narrower instance within the established domain, not a new area.

### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to convert deterministic AI forecasts into calibrated probabilistic ensembles by exploiting anisotropy. Paper [1] explicitly aims to transform deterministic neural network weather forecasting systems into ensemble forecasting systems, which aligns with the same objective at the problem-class level. Paper [6] also addresses calibration of probabilistic forecasts from deterministic models, which matches the purpose of converting deterministic outputs into calibrated probabilistic ensembles. Paper [12] introduces a method to generate probabilistic forecasts from deterministic models, which is substantively equivalent to the stated purpose. Therefore, the purpose is **covered**.

### Mechanism
The mechanism, Anisotropic Spectral Error Dressing (ASED), extends spectral error dressing by modeling within-degree anisotropy via mu-binning across degree bands and redistributing variance across orders while preserving the degree spectrum. Paper [13] discusses ensemble dressing of meteorological fields using spatial regression to estimate uncertainty, which involves redistributing uncertainty across spatial dimensions, a conceptually similar primitive. Paper [16] introduces a general weighting theory for ensemble learning that leverages spectral and geometric structure, which overlaps with the spectral redistribution aspect of ASED. Paper [18] develops stochastic and deterministic energy backscatter schemes that redistribute energy across spectral scales, which is analogous to redistributing variance across orders in ASED. Thus, the mechanism is **covered**.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses an odd/even month calibration/evaluation split with 354 forecasts and requires no model retraining beyond bin weights. Paper [6] employs a calibration method for probabilistic forecasts, which involves adjusting probability distributions to achieve long-term calibration, a substantively equivalent evaluation design. Paper [11] uses statistical post-processing models to correct biases and dispersion errors in ensemble forecasts, which aligns with the evaluation design of validating calibration quality. Paper [20] employs ensemble model output statistics (EMOS) for calibrating ensemble forecasts, which similarly validates calibration quality. Therefore, the evaluation design is **covered**.

### Domain
The domain is ensemble generation and post-processing for AI weather models. Paper [1] explicitly addresses ensemble generation for neural network-based weather forecasts, which matches the domain. Paper [2] focuses on ensemble forecasting for AI-based weather models, which is substantively equivalent. Paper [5] discusses ensemble weather forecasting using diffusion models, which also falls within the same domain. Paper [9] addresses ensemble prediction systems for weather forecasting, which aligns with the domain. Therefore, the domain is **covered**.
